{{Short description|Transformation in quantum mechanics}}
{{refimprove|date=July 2023}}
In [[quantum mechanics]], the '''Holstein–Primakoff transformation''' is a [[Map (mathematics)|mapping]] from [[boson]] [[creation and annihilation operators]] to the [[Spin (physics)|spin]] [[Operator (mathematics)|operators]], effectively truncating their infinite-dimensional [[Fock space]] to finite-dimensional subspaces.

One important aspect of quantum mechanics is the occurrence of—in general—[[non-commuting]] [[Operator (mathematics)|operators]] which represent [[observables]], quantities that can be measured.
A standard example of a set of such operators are the three components of the [[angular momentum]] operators, which are crucial in many quantum systems.
These operators are complicated, and one would like to find a simpler representation, which can be used to generate approximate calculational schemes.

The transformation was developed<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Holstein | first1=T. | last2=Primakoff | first2=H. |author-link2=Henry Primakoff| title=Field Dependence of the Intrinsic Domain Magnetization of a Ferromagnet | journal=Physical Review | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=58 | issue=12 | date=1940-12-15 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/physrev.58.1098 | pages=1098–1113| bibcode=1940PhRv...58.1098H }}</ref> in 1940 by [[Theodore Holstein]], a graduate student at the time,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://texts.cdlib.org/view?docId=hb767nb3z6&doc.view=frames&chunk.id=div00052&toc.depth=1&toc.id=|title=Theodore D. Holstein, Physics: Los Angeles|publisher=University of California|access-date=23 December 2015}}</ref> and [[Henry Primakoff]]. This method has found widespread applicability and has been extended in many different directions.

There is a close link to other methods of boson mapping of operator algebras: in particular, the (non-Hermitian) [[Freeman Dyson|Dyson]]–Maleev<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Klein | first1=Abraham | last2=Marshalek | first2=E. R. | title=Boson realizations of Lie algebras with applications to nuclear physics | journal=Reviews of Modern Physics | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=63 | issue=2 | date=1991-04-01 | issn=0034-6861 | doi=10.1103/revmodphys.63.375 | pages=375–558| bibcode=1991RvMP...63..375K }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=This Week's Citation Classic by F. J. Dyson, August 4, 1986|journal=Current Contents|date=8 Sep 1986|issue=36|page=16|url=http://www.garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1986/A1986D731300001.pdf}}</ref> technique, and to a lesser extent the [[Jordan map|Jordan&ndash;Schwinger map]].<ref>[[Julian Schwinger|Schwinger, J.]] (1952). [http://www.osti.gov/cgi-bin/rd_accomplishments/display_biblio.cgi?id=ACC0111&numPages=92&fp=N "On Angular Momentum"], Unpublished Report, Harvard University, Nuclear Development Associates, Inc., [[United States Department of Energy]] (through predecessor agency the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]]),  Report Number  NYO-3071 (January 26, 1952).</ref>  There is, furthermore,  a close link to the theory of (generalized) [[coherent states]] in [[Lie algebras]].

==Description==
The basic idea can be illustrated for the basic example of spin operators of quantum mechanics.

For any set of right-handed orthogonal axes, define the components of this [[vector operator]] as <math>S_x</math>, <math>S_y</math> and <math>S_z</math>, which are mutually [[noncommuting]], i.e., <math>\left[S_x,S_y\right] = i\hbar S_z</math> and its cyclic permutations.

In order to uniquely specify the states of a spin, one may diagonalise any set of commuting operators. Normally one uses the SU(2) [[Casimir element|Casimir operators]] <math>S^2</math> and <math>S_z</math>, which leads  to
states with the [[quantum numbers]] <math>\left|s,m_s\right\rangle</math>,
:<math>S^2\left|s,m_s\right\rangle=\hbar^2 s(s+1) \left|s,m_s\right\rangle,</math>
:<math>S_z\left|s,m_s\right\rangle=\hbar m_s\left|s,m_s\right\rangle.</math>
The projection quantum number <math>m_s</math> takes on all the values <math> (-s, -s+1, \ldots ,s-1,  s) </math>.

Consider a single particle of spin {{mvar|s}}  (i.e., look at a single [[irreducible representation]] of SU(2)). Now take the state with maximal projection <math>\left|s,m_s= +s\right\rangle</math>, the [[Weight (representation theory)#Highest-weight module|extremal weight state]] as a vacuum for a set of boson operators, and each subsequent state with lower projection quantum number as a boson excitation of the previous one,
:<math>\left|s,s-n\right\rangle\mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt{n!}}\left(a^\dagger\right)^n|0\rangle_B   ~.</math>

Each additional boson then corresponds to a decrease of {{math|''ħ''}}  in the spin projection. Thus, the spin raising and lowering operators 
<math>S_+= S_x + i S_y</math> and <math>S_- = S_x - i S_y</math>, so that <math>[S_+,S_-]=2\hbar S_z</math>, correspond (in the sense detailed below) to the bosonic annihilation and creation operators, respectively.
The precise relations between the operators must be chosen to ensure the correct commutation relations for the  spin operators, such that they act on a finite-dimensional space, unlike the original Fock space.

The resulting Holstein–Primakoff transformation can be written as
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation =  <math>S_+ = \hbar \sqrt{2s} \sqrt{1-\frac{a^\dagger a}{2s}}\, a ~, \qquad
S_- = \hbar \sqrt{2s} a^\dagger\, \sqrt{1-\frac{a^\dagger a}{2s}} ~, \qquad 
S_z = \hbar(s - a^\dagger a) ~.</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0070BF
|bgcolor=#FAFFFB}}
The transformation is particularly useful in the case where {{mvar|s}} is large, when the square roots can be expanded as [[Taylor series]], to give an expansion in decreasing powers of  {{mvar|s}}.

Alternatively to a Taylor expansion there has been recent progress <ref name = "Fiete">{{cite journal | last1=Vogl | first1=Michael | last2=Laurell | first2=Pontus | last3=Zhang | first3=Hao | last4=Okamoto | first4=Satoshi | last5=Fiete | first5=Gregory A. | title=Resummation of the Holstein-Primakoff expansion and differential equation approach to operator square roots | journal=Physical Review Research | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=2 | issue=4 | date=2020-11-17 | issn=2643-1564 | doi=10.1103/physrevresearch.2.043243 | article-number=043243| arxiv=2006.06871 | bibcode=2020PhRvR...2d3243V | s2cid=219635834 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Hucht">{{cite journal | last1=König | first1=Jürgen | last2=Hucht | first2=Alfred | title=Newton series expansion of bosonic operator functions | journal=SciPost Physics | publisher=Stichting SciPost | volume=10 | issue=1 | date=2021-01-13 | issn=2542-4653 | doi=10.21468/scipostphys.10.1.007 | page=007| arxiv=2008.11139 | bibcode=2021ScPP...10....7K | s2cid=221293056 | doi-access=free }}</ref>  with a [[resummation]] of the series that made expressions possible that are polynomial in bosonic operators but still mathematically exact (on the physical subspace). The first method develops a resummation method <ref name="Fiete"/> that is '''exact''' for spin <math>s=1/2</math>, while the latter<ref name="Hucht"/> employs a [[Newton series]] (a finite difference) expansion with an identical result, as shown below

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation =  <math>S_+^{(1/2)}= \hbar \sqrt{2s}\left[1+\left(\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2 s}}-1\right)a^\dagger a\right]a, \qquad
S_-^{(1/2)} = (S_+^{(1/2)})^\dagger, \qquad 
S_z^{(1/2)} = \hbar(s - a^\dagger a) ~.</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0070BF
|bgcolor=#FAFFFB}}

While the expression above is not exact for spins higher than 1/2 it is an improvement over the Taylor series. Exact expressions also exist for higher spins and include <math>2s+1</math> terms. Much like the result above also for the expressions of higher spins <math>S_+ = S_-^\dagger</math> and therefore the resummation is hermitian.

There also exists a non-Hermitian '''Dyson–Maleev''' (by [[Freeman Dyson]] and S.V. Maleev) variant realization '''''J''''' is related to the above and valid for all spins, 
:<math>
J_+ = \hbar \, a ~, \qquad
J_-=  S_- ~  \sqrt{2s-a^\dagger a} = \hbar  a^\dagger\, (2s-a^\dagger a)~, \qquad
J_z=S_z = \hbar(s - a^\dagger a) ~,
</math>
satisfying the same commutation relations and characterized by the same Casimir invariant.

The technique can be further extended to the [[Witt algebra]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fairlie | first1=D.B. |author-link1=David Fairlie| last2=Nuyts | first2=J. | last3=Zachos | first3=C.K. | title=Construction of classical Virasoro algebras as SU(1,1) extensions | journal=Physics Letters B | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=202 | issue=3 | year=1988 | issn=0370-2693 | doi=10.1016/0370-2693(88)90478-9 | pages=320–324| bibcode=1988PhLB..202..320F }}</ref> which is the centerless [[Virasoro algebra]].
